description: Python's rjust zero-pads an order number that follows its source
code:
order = "7"
number = order.rjust(4, "0")
assert(number, "0007")
order = "42"
number

description: Python's ljust fills a report column with dots up to its width
code:
item = "tea"
cell = item.ljust(6, ".")
assert(cell, "tea...")
item = "honey"
cell

description: C#'s PadLeft right-aligns a price in a column of six characters
code:
price = "4.5"
cell = price.PadLeft(6)
assert(cell, "   4.5")
price = "120.25"
cell

description: C#'s PadRight repeats a fill of two characters and cuts its last copy
code:
code = "ab"
shown = code.PadRight(7, "xy")
assert(shown, "abxyxyx")
code = "abcde"
shown

description: Ruby's rule repeats and cuts a longer fill on either side
A class-level rule gives every ticket a zero-padded code that follows its id
code:
class Ticket(id):
    this.id = id
$Ticket.code = "T-" + String($Ticket.id).rjust(4, "0")
t = Ticket(7)
assert(t.code, "T-0007")
t.id = 42
t.code

description: A mapped list of labels pads every pushed name to one width
code:
names = ["ab", "c"]
labels = names.map(n -> n.ljust(3, "_"))
assert(labels, ["ab_", "c__"])
names.push("dddd")
labels

description: Padding counts characters, so an accented name and an emoji take one place each
A width too large to pad raises the padding error and the failed update rolls back
code:
width = 3
code = "7".rjust(width, "0")
try:
    width = 1 / 0
catch error:
    assert(error, TypeError("Padded string is too large"))
[width, code]

description: An empty fill and a width the text already reaches leave the text as it is
Widths convert as repeat counts, so a fraction truncates and a negative width pads nothing
An explanation quotes a padding alias as it is written
code:
label = "7"
width = 3
code = label.rjust(width, "0")
assert(code, "007")
(why code).map(step -> step.rule)
